sections.body_md:
The eigenvalues of the system matrix \(A\) are the modes of the free response. Each eigenvalue contributes a term to the solution: \(e^{\lambda t}\) for a simple eigenvalue, \(t^k e^{\lambda t}\) for repeated ones. The eigenvectors determine how the initial condition excites each mode.

A real negative eigenvalue gives exponential decay. A complex conjugate pair gives damped oscillation. The time constant is the reciprocal of the real-part magnitude. The imaginary part is the oscillation frequency. Stability requires all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Free response: \(x(t) = e^{At} x(0)\).

Diagonalizable case: \(A = V \Lambda V^{-1}\), so \(e^{At} = V e^{\Lambda t} V^{-1}\).

Mode from eigenvalue \(\lambda = \sigma + j\omega\): decays at rate \(|\sigma|\), oscillates at \(\omega\).

Natural frequency: \(\omega_n = |\lambda|\). Damping ratio: \(\zeta = |\sigma|/\omega_n\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Consider \(A\) with eigenvalues \(-2\) and \(-1 \pm 3j\). The real eigenvalue at \(-2\) contributes \(c_1 e^{-2t}\). The complex pair contributes \(e^{-t}(c_2 \cos 3t + c_3 \sin 3t)\). The mode at \(-2\) has time constant 0.5 s. The oscillatory mode has time constant 1 s and frequency 3 rad/s. After 3 s (six time constants of the fast mode), the \(-2\) mode is at \(e^{-6} = 0.0025\) and the response is dominated by the slower oscillating mode.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The eigenvalue's imaginary part is the oscillation frequency in rad/s, not the time constant. Repeated eigenvalues may have \(t e^{\lambda t}\) terms; check the Jordan form. Diagonalization fails if eigenvectors are not independent. Computing \(e^{At}\) element-wise is wrong; use the spectral decomposition.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Reachability asks which initial conditions each mode can be driven to. Observability asks which modes appear in the output. State feedback places eigenvalues. Observers estimate modes that are not directly measured. The eigenvalue-eigenvector decomposition is the foundation of modal analysis.
